newsitem.title: USA: Three games for aspiring Pinball Wizards.
newsitem.headline: Three games for aspiring Pinball Wizards.

text.p: The game of pinball has a long and curious history. It probably first appeared as an upright box where a ball was dropped from the top. Pins or pegs in the box determined how the ball fell and how many points a player earned when it finally rested in a well at the bottom.
Today's pinball machines, first produced in the early 1930s, never had any pins, but somehow the name stuck.

The machines were banned in New York City in 1942 because they were regarded as games of chance, a ban that lasted as late as 1976. The belief that the machines encouraged gambling prompted many states to ban the ones that gave free games, a limitation that manufacturers learned to circumvent by allowing players to earn an extra ball.

Although pinball was disparaged by grown-ups as a waste of time and money, avid players knew better. It took skill to nudge the machine enough to keep the ball from missing the flippers, but not too much to have the dreaded "Tilt" sign light up.
Today, pinball machines seem headed for extinction. They often sit unused and unappreciated in arcades while video games suck up all the quarters.

Although computer games makers seem intent on keeping pinball alive, they face the problem of trying to pack all the detail of a pinball machine game onto a computer screen, which has the wrong shape. Maxis, Sierra and Interplay are the latest companies to give it a whirl.
Maxis' "Full Tilt! Pinball 2" ($30) may be the best choice.
Instead of trying to squeeze a long table onto the screen, "Full Tilt!" shortens and fattens the table to fit everything in.

It has three games: "Alien Daze," which has a UFO theme, "Mad Scientist" where balls can dissolve in a poisonous vat, and "Captain Hero," where animated villains pop up on the game board and the hero is "At-Man," named after the circular "at" symbol common to Internet addresses.
The game is versatile, allowing players to control the music and sound effects if they become annoying. The animations that pop up in the game give it an extra dimension.
Sierra's "3-D Ultra Pinball: Creep Night" is also a good choice, but it costs a hefty $20 more.

"Creep Night," doesn't even try to reproduce a table with conventional dimensions. Instead, the three tables in the game are wide and squat. Each has three separate playing areas -- the corner ones are sometimes so tight, you find yourself incessantly pushing the flipper button to avoid losing the ball. The music and sound effects are easier on the ear, but the ball is about 25 percent smaller than the pinball on the "Full Tilt!" tables.
If you can beat the three regular tables -- the castle courtyard, the mad scientist's lab and the dungeon catacombs -- there's a bonus table. But only real pinball wizards can get there.

Interplay's "Pro Pinball" has an intermediate price of $40 and proportions that are closer to a real pinball table. And while all three games work with Windows, "Pro Pinball" is also available for the Macintosh.

Unfortunately, the table is not as complex, with only three flippers vs. as many as seven in "Creep Night." "Pro Pinball" boasts of six different views of the table, but they don't vary significantly. Your choice simply affects the width at the base and how much of the display screen is visible at the head of the machine. Finally, there's only one table to choose from, although Interplay claims there are four "missions" within the game.
"Pro Pinball's" chief advantage is that you can play up to six balls simultaneously, which makes for a wild game. The most I saw in "Full Tilt!" and "Creep Night" was two balls.
All three games, with their detailed graphics and the ability to "nudge" the table in various ways, illustrate how good computerized pinball has become.
It makes you wonder if real-life pinball machines are soon to become history.

One theme song for the software business should be "Promises, Promises." Companies are constantly being forced to delay the release of new products beyond the promised debut. Often it's because bugs have cropped up.
But VR Sports, which originally promised to release its "VR Baseball" game in 1995, has come out with a Top Ten list to explain why we may not see it until the first pitch this spring:
10. Marketing is complaining there isn't enough blood and guts in the game.
9. An EA virus has been detected in VR Baseball which causes players to purposely throw a game.
8. Have not been able to get the game to boot since implementing the "Players' Strike" feature.
7. Two words: Nomo Mania.
6. There was a setback in testing because many of the testers were using illegally corked joysticks.
5. It takes way too many polygons to represent major-league umpires.
4. Stupidly hired "Codeless" Joe Jackson as lead programmer.
3. Many programmers were found aimlessly roaming through corn fields saying, "If you programme it, it will crash."
2. Programmers and artists can't continue without a collective bargaining agreement.
1. Took too long to abandon the "We can save money by using the old source code for Pong" theory.
(Gene Emery is a columnist who covers science and technology. His Internet address is gene.emery(at)prodigy.com. Any opinions in the column are his alone.)
